steps.question: What condition is imposed on the average loss after the names example?

steps.question: Why does pointwise decrease of the candidate function not guarantee that condition?
steps.answer_text: Being decreasing only rewards assigning more probability to each observed outcome considered separately. It does not ensure that, under the normalization constraint on Q, the expected P-weighted score is uniquely optimized by reproducing the full distribution P; that stronger property is strict propriety.
steps.why: This follows from the transcript distinction between the local monotonic constraint at 1329.1–1339.7 and the later distribution-level minimum requirement, together with general knowledge of proper scoring rules.

answer: The supplied transcript never states the names or formulas of the three non-logarithmic curves drawn earlier, so I cannot name them without guessing from information that was only on screen. What the transcript does establish is why mere decrease is insufficient: the relevant objective is the P-weighted average of F(Q), and it must have its minimum exactly when the whole predicted distribution Q equals the empirical distribution P. A decreasing F only gives the pointwise preference 'higher probability for the observed token means lower loss'; it does not guarantee this distribution-level, uniquely truthful optimum under the constraint that the Q values sum to one. For example, from general knowledge, the decreasing loss F(q)=1-q would minimize expected loss by concentrating Q on a most frequent outcome rather than by setting Q=P. Thus the needed condition is that the scoring rule be strictly proper, which negative logarithmic loss satisfies.
